raw_response:
## Recommendation

My first candidate is **Laravel with Livewire**, provided your existing PHP business logic can be separated from the old pages and reused. I would also seriously consider **Vue 3 over your existing PHP/Perl backend**: that narrower migration could be the better route if preserving the current server behavior is the main way to finish quickly. This is an engineering judgment about migration scope, not a measured claim that either framework is universally fastest.

The important unknown is where the business logic lives. Replacing templates is quite different from extracting rules that are mixed into PHP pages, jQuery handlers and Perl scripts. None of the public framework documentation can establish compatibility with that unseen code.

### Ranked options

**1. Laravel with Livewire, plus JavaScript for the grouping workspace.** This is my starting point for a PHP-centered rebuild. Laravel's [frontend guide](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/frontend) documents reactive PHP components through Livewire and a route to authentication scaffolding. The [Livewire 2 quickstart](https://laravel-livewire.com/docs/2.x/quickstart) shows the PHP-class/Blade-view model. Its [Alpine integration guide](https://laravel-livewire.com/docs/2.x/alpine-js) also describes keeping small browser interactions local.

I would put the retained domain operations behind a clear service boundary, then have the new application call them. Dragging should have immediate browser feedback; saving the resulting group membership should invoke the server's validated operation. This needs integration code. The documentation does not show that your existing PHP or Perl can simply be dropped into Laravel. For the historical Laravel 9 option, [the release notes](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/releases) specify PHP 8.0 or newer, so the actual legacy runtime is an early compatibility check.

**2. Vue 3 while retaining the existing backend.** Vue is a good candidate if the largest change is the interactive component/group editor. Its [adoption guide](https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/ways-of-using-vue.html) documents adding Vue to server-rendered pages and embedding components in legacy applications. You can therefore start with one workspace rather than first reconstructing all server behavior.

This is a frontend contribution, not the entire server application. The existing account, database, prepaid-entitlement and export operations would need a dependable interface. My proposed mapping is: load the user's selected components, manage the browser interaction in Vue, and send validated change requests to the existing domain operations. If those operations cannot be separated from the old rendering code, the apparent small migration becomes a backend extraction project. That is the main fact to establish before selecting this route.

**3. Laravel with Inertia.js and Vue.** Prefer this over the Livewire approach if the component editor needs considerable browser-side state and you want to build it as Vue pages. Laravel's [Inertia documentation](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/frontend#inertia) describes connecting server routes and controllers to Vue or React components, with the server supplying page data.

This is an alternative stack, not an additional layer you automatically need on top of Livewire. It adds a Vue/component and asset-tooling learning path. Whether that effort pays off depends on the actual grouping interface; the question does not tell us whether it is a few sortable lists or a much more elaborate editor. The existing-business-logic migration remains unresolved.

**4. Symfony with Symfony UX.** This is another PHP framework route worth considering. The [Symfony 6.2 UX overview](https://symfony.com/doc/6.2/frontend/ux.html) describes Stimulus-based integration and packages for Chart.js, Turbo, Live Components and Vue.

I rank it as an alternative rather than the first migration to try because nothing in the question indicates existing Symfony experience, and this research did not establish a smaller migration than the options above. It still requires a plan for calling the old domain operations and implementing the application-specific grouping, export and prepaid workflows.

### How the named features fit

| Existing behavior | Proposed implementation boundary |
|---|---|
| Store many selected components and groups per account | Keep the domain rules and database ownership checks on the server; adapt the chosen framework around those operations. |
| Drag and drop between groups | Use a browser interaction component, then persist the resulting operation through the server. [Sortable's official README](https://github.com/SortableJS/Sortable/blob/master/README.md) documents movement between lists, group configuration and drop/update callbacks. It is a supporting library, not a replacement for the application framework. |
| Usage graphs | Calculate the intended usage statistics using the retained business rules. Symfony UX's documented Chart.js integration is one available rendering route; equivalent integration in the other stacks remains application work. |
| Excel export | Preserve the current exporter if it still meets the requirement. If it needs replacement, [PhpSpreadsheet](https://phpspreadsheet.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) documents PHP writers for XLSX and XLS. Its consulted live requirements are not evidence of the package's requirements in January 2023. |
| Prepaid service | Preserve the existing entitlement and payment semantics. “Prepaid” does not tell us whether this means subscriptions, credits, time-limited access or something else, so I would not select a billing package from that description alone. |

“Up to thousands” also needs careful interpretation: the question describes stored selections, not necessarily thousands of visible draggable elements. I would build a representative account-to-grouping-to-save-to-export slice and measure it with realistic data. Search, pagination or windowed rendering may be appropriate design choices, but this research did not verify a ready-made implementation for any candidate. Do not interpret a drag-and-drop demo as proof of acceptable performance at your scale.

### Decision and limits

Start with the retained business operations and prototype one real grouping workflow. If they fit naturally behind a new PHP application, try Laravel with Livewire first. If the existing server interfaces already work and the interface is the principal problem, the Vue-only migration may have the smaller initial scope. If the editor needs extensive local state, compare the Vue route with Laravel/Inertia/Vue.

All four are **documented architectural candidates**, but my end-to-end judgment is **INSUFFICIENT for an unconditional fit** because preservation of the particular existing business logic is not verified. None has an established decisive violation; uncertainty is not a reason to discard it. One useful next confirmation is whether the same representative business operation can be called through the proposed boundary with unchanged results. A successful mapping supports retaining that candidate; an unavoidable loss of required behavior excludes that migration design.

The question is dated January 10, 2023. Laravel 9's release date is February 8, 2022, and the [Vue 3 announcement](https://blog.vuejs.org/posts/vue-3-one-piece) is dated September 18, 2020. Most other sources consulted are live pages with unknown publication/update dates, including versioned documentation. They support the described architectures but do not establish an exact January 2023 dependency set or feature snapshot. I have not installed, run, benchmarked or integrated these frameworks.
